units.translation: On accent and declension see the passages of the grammarians cited in the Thesaurus vol. 8 p. 1384. The regular declension is χειρός χειρί χείρα χεῖρε χεροῖν χεῖρες χερῶν χεῖρας, with the first syllable long where the second is short, and short where the second is long; but the poets also say χερός χερί χέρα χέρε χέρες χέρας and χειρῶν when the metre demands. Against this rule the copyists and perhaps the writers themselves not infrequently err, especially in the genitive plural, which, except for those passages of the poets that require the iambic measure, is now almost consistently written χειρῶν in poetry as well as prose, although reason demands that it follow the same law as the genitive dual, which Choeroboscus in Theodos. p. 346 has most correctly observed to be χεροῖν for the most part, rarely χειρον. The dative plural χερσί, not χειρσί, is rightly noted by the ancient grammarians. For the diphthong is admitted only in the trisyllabic form, χείρεσιν in Homer Il. 20, 468 ήπτετο χείρεσι γούνων [he clasped his knees with his hands], and much more frequently χείρεσσι in epic and lyric poets, rarely in tragic poets, as χείρεσσι and χείρεσσιν in Sophocles in lyric passages Ant. 976 1297, never in Aeschylus.

which verse, together with the preceding ones, we owe to the scholiast on Euripides Alcest. 768, where similarly οὐδ᾽ ἐξέτεινα χεῖρ᾽ ἀποιμώζων ἐμὴν δέσποιναν [nor did I stretch out my hand, lamenting my mistress], on which the scholiast says σεσημείωται ὅτι καὶ Αἰσχύλος ὡς γινόμενον τοῦτο συνίστησιν ἐν ταῖς Χοηφόροις [it has been noted that Aeschylus also presents this as happening in the Choephori], and in another scholium ἔθος γὰρ ἦν ἐκτείνειν τὰς χεῖρας, ὅταν ἐκφορά νεκροῦ γίνηται [for it was the custom to stretch out the hands whenever a corpse was carried out].

where the scholiast notes χειρὶ [with hand] as the full form, which should be written either χεῖρε [two hands] or, more probably, χεῖρα [hand], just as in the verse of the Choephori just cited οὐδ᾽ ἐξέτεινα χεῖρ᾽ [nor did I stretch out my hand] the scholiast on Euripides correctly took χεῖρ᾽ [hand] for χειρα [hand].
